{{Short description|Multivariate statistical technique}}

{{Orphan|date=June 2025}}
'''Spatial Principal Component Analysis''' ('''sPCA''') is a multivariate statistical technique that complements the traditional [[Principal Component Analysis]] (PCA) by incorporating spatial information into the analysis of genetic variation. While traditional PCA can be used to find spatial patterns,<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Demšar |first1=Urška |last2=Harris |first2=Paul |last3=Brunsdon |first3=Chris |last4=Fotheringham |first4=A. Stewart |last5=McLoone |first5=Sean |date=2013-01-01 |title=Principal Component Analysis on Spatial Data: An Overview |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/00045608.2012.689236 |journal=Annals of the Association of American Geographers |volume=103 |issue=1 |pages=106–128 |doi=10.1080/00045608.2012.689236 |bibcode=2013AAAG..103..106D |issn=0004-5608|url-access=subscription }}</ref> it focuses on reducing data dimensionality by identifying uncorrelated principal components that capture maximum variance, thus often lacking power to identify non-trivial spatial genetic patterns.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite book |last=Jombart |first=Thibaut |title=A tutorial for the spatial Analysis of Principal Components (sPCA) using adegenet 2.0.0 |date=2015-06-23 |publisher=Imperial College London, MRC Centre for Outbreak Analysis and Modelling |publication-date=2015 |language=english }}</ref> By accounting for [[spatial autocorrelation]], sPCA is able to uncover spatial patterns in the data and find the spatial structure of datasets where observations are either geographically or topologically linked. This statistical power improvement allows the investigation of cryptic spatial patterns of genetic variability otherwise overlooked.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Jombart |first1=T |last2=Devillard |first2=S |last3=Dufour |first3=A-B |last4=Pontier |first4=D |date=July 2008 |title=Revealing cryptic spatial patterns in genetic variability by a new multivariate method |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/hdy200834 |journal=Heredity |language=en |volume=101 |issue=1 |pages=92–103 |doi=10.1038/hdy.2008.34 |pmid=18446182 |bibcode=2008Hered.101...92J |issn=0018-067X}}</ref>

sPCA has been applied in various fields, including [[geography]], [[ecology]] and [[genetics]].<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4" /><ref name=":5" /><ref name=":6" />

== History ==
sPCA was introduced in 2008 by Thibaut Jombart, Sébastien Devillard, Anne-Béatrice Dufour, and D. Pontier as a spatially explicit method to investigate the spatial pattern of [[genetic variation]] among individuals or populations.<ref name=":1" />

In 2017, Valeria Montano and Thibaut Jombart published an alternative non-parametric test to evaluate the significance of global and local spatial genetic patterns with improved statistical power.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Montano |first1=V. |last2=Jombart |first2=T. |date=2017-12-16 |title=An Eigenvalue test for spatial principal component analysis |journal=BMC Bioinformatics |volume=18 |issue=1 |page=562 |doi=10.1186/s12859-017-1988-y |doi-access=free |issn=1471-2105 |pmc=5732370 |pmid=29246102 |bibcode=2017BMCBi..18..562M }}</ref>

== Details ==
sPCA modifies the PCA framework by integrating [[Spatial weight matrix|spatial weights]], typically in the form of connectivity matrices or spatial adjacency graphs. It identifies principal components (PCs) that maximize both genentic variance and spatial autocorreation, as measured by [[Moran's I]].<ref name=":2" /> These weights represent relationships between observations based on geographic distance or other spatial criteria.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Li |first1=J. |last2=Reich |first2=B.J. |last3=Bondell |first3=H.D. |title=Extending principal component analysis for spatially correlated data |journal=BMC Bioinformatics |date=2017 |volume=18 |issue=1 |page=562 |doi=10.1186/s12859-017-1988-y|doi-access=free |pmid=29246102 |pmc=5732370 |bibcode=2017BMCBi..18..562M }}</ref> The method decomposes variance into two components:

* '''Global structures''', correspond to positive autocorrelation, that is, reflect broad-scale spatial patterns where similar values cluster over large regions.
* '''Local structures''', correspond to negative autocorrelation, that is, capture fine-scale spatial variations or localized patterns.

The core of sPCA relies on the eigenanalysis of a spatially weighted covariance or correlation matrix. The spatial weight matrix can be constructed using techniques such as [[Delaunay triangulation]], [[Nearest neighbor graph|nearest-neighbor graphs]], or distance-based criteria.

Applications of sPCA should be used only as an explorative tool.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" />

== Software/Source Code ==
sPCA implementations are available in [[R (programming language)|R]] in <code>adegenet</code> and <code>ntbox</code> .<ref>{{Cite web |title=R: Spatial principal component analysis |url=https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/adegenet/html/spca.html |access-date=2025-03-03 |website=search.r-project.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=spca: spca: Principal Component Analysis for Spatial Data in luismurao/ntbox: From Getting Biodiversity Data to Evaluating Species Distribution Models in a Friendly GUI Environment |url=https://rdrr.io/github/luismurao/ntbox/man/spca.html |access-date=2025-03-03 |website=rdrr.io |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=spca_randtest: Monte Carlo test for sPCA in adegenet: Exploratory Analysis of Genetic and Genomic Data |url=https://rdrr.io/cran/adegenet/man/spca_randtest.html |access-date=2025-03-03 |website=rdrr.io |language=en}}</ref>

These tools facilitate the application of sPCA by providing functions for constructing spatial weight matrices, performing eigenanalysis, and obtaining spatial principal components in an easy-to-read form.
